transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Cora Coleman.
Democrats have flipped control of Congress in the midterm elections.
They picked up seven more seats in the Senate, two races still to be called, and they claimed
about two dozen House seats with dozens of races there uncalled.
The outstanding Senate races are in Alaska and Mississippi.
In Alaska, Republican incumbent Senator Dan Sullivan has a slight lead over Democratic
challenger Mary Peltola.
In Mississippi, Democratic challenger Scott Colombe has a slight lead over GOP incumbent
Cindy Hyde-Smith.
Many voters who chose Democratic candidates cited the high cost of living and President
Trump's decisions to launch the war against Iran and to impose tariffs on many countries.
President Trump had barnstormed through several states before the election.
He repeatedly told Republicans to vote as if he were, quote, "on the ballot."
Last night on Fox News, Trump said Republicans did poorly because he was not on the ballot.
You know, I don't like to consider it a defeat for me.
I was on the ballot.
If you're on the ballot, it's different than if you're not on the ballot.
But nevertheless, you know, I feel badly for a lot of very good Republicans.
Trump did congratulate Democrats on their wins.
National Democrats have an ambitious agenda of investigations planned for their return
to power next year.
And Pierre's Eric McDaniel reports they're likely to focus on issues including war and
corruption.
A return to majority status means that Democrats will have robust investigatory powers at
their disposal, including the ability to compel individuals to testify before lawmakers.
The party has a broad set of probes planned, including the extent of the president's connections
to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, perceived intermingling of the president's
duties and financial interests, high profile acts of violence by federal immigration enforcement
personnel and the U.S.-Iran War, which has never been authorized by Congress.
Democrats argue that that's in contravention of the Constitution, which gives Congress
the sole power to regulate military conflict.
The Trump administration has a record of minimal cooperation with the legislative branch, Eric
McDaniel and Pierre News in Washington.
GOP candidates won several seats yesterday that Republicans redrew earlier to favor GOP
candidates in elections.
And Pierre's Katherine Welch is in Orlando.
She tracked one such congressional district, Florida's 9th.
It's just south of Orlando, near the theme parks, and that district was pretty much centered
on Osceola County, which has about 55 percent Latino voters.
It was redrawn to stretch across a number of mostly rural counties and was consistently
expected to favor the Republican candidate.
But the Democratic incumbent Darren Soto held on to the seat despite its dramatic change.
NPR's Katherine Welch reporting from Orlando, Florida.
You're listening to NPR.
Investors seem very buoyed by the midterm election news.
On Wall Street in pre-market trading, the Dow Jones industrial average is up more than
800 points, more than one and a half percent.
Both the tech-heavy NASDAQ and the broader S&P 500 indices are up strongly.
North Korea has launched multiple missiles in its fourth such test in a week.
Pyongyang seems to have another message.
And PR's Anthony Kuhn reports from Seoul the message may be that resuming dialogue with
the U.S. is still possible.
South Korea's military says the missiles were launched from the East Coast and flew eastward
into the sea.
This follows launches of rocket artillery and cluster bombs mounted on tactical ballistic
missiles and cruise missiles in the past week.
Meanwhile, North Korean leader Kim Jong-un's sister Kim Yo-jong said in a statement carried
by state media that talks with the U.S. are still possible but not necessary for the North's
national interests.
She added that Pyongyang sees no need to sit face to face with unreliable and hostile counterparts.
Anthony Kuhn in PR News, Seoul.
European investigators have not been able to find who hacked into supermarket freezers
in several countries this week.
The saboteurs boosted the heat in the refrigerators in the freezers, often to more than 120 degrees.
Spoiled food had to be thrown out, costing grocers millions of dollars.
This is the second time this has happened to European grocery stores in recent weeks.
I'm Corva Coleman, NPR News, from Washington.

topics.text: Democrats flip control of Congress in midterm elections, with Senate races in Alaska and Mississippi still uncalled
Trump says Republicans did poorly because he was not on the ballot, speaking on Fox News
Democrats plan investigations into Epstein connections, presidential finances, immigration enforcement violence, and the Iran war
Florida's 9th District Democrat Darren Soto holds seat despite Republican-favoring redistricting
Dow Jones jumps over 800 points in premarket trading after midterm election results
North Korea launches multiple missiles in fourth test in a week, as Kim Yo-jong says talks with U.S. remain possible
European investigators unable to identify hackers who sabotaged supermarket freezers across several countries
